title: Lumbar Puncture and CNS Involvement in Herpes Zoster of the Trigeminal Region: A Bicenter Comparison Including a 10-Year Evolution
summary:
Shingles in the face and neck is a condition caused by the reactivation of a virus that has been dormant in the body. This virus can not only cause the typical rash but may also lead to serious problems if it affects the nervous system. These complications can include inflammation in the brain, spinal cord, or nerve roots, which can have severe health consequences.
Doctors recommend testing the fluid around the brain and spinal cord if there is suspicion that the nervous system is involve (such as in cases of severe headaches, stiff neck, or sensitivity to light). Interestingly, studies show that up to 60% of people with shingles in the face or neck have abnormalities in this fluid, even if they don’t show any noticeable neurological symptoms.
Because symptoms and decisions about such tests vary widely, there is no standardized approach to diagnosis and treatment. The goal of this study is to examine when and why doctors perform this fluid test, determine how often it actually reveals nervous system involvement, and compare how these practices have changed over the past decade (2012–2014 vs. 2022–2024).
Ultimately, the study aims to evaluate current diagnostic methods and, if necessary, identify ways to improve treatment practices.

interventions.name: Retrospective analysis of all patients who were hospitalized with a diagnosis of herpes zoster at RWTH Aachen University Hospital and the University Hospital of Cologne between 2022 and 2024.
Retrospective analysis of all patients who were hospitalized with a diagnosis of herpes zoster at RWTH Aachen University Hospital and the University Hospital of Cologne between 2012 and 2014.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
All patients who were hospitalized at RWTH Aachen University Hospital and Cologne University Hospital between 2022 and 2024 and between 2012 and 2014 with a diagnosis of herpes zoster (ICD-10: B02) and who had involvement of the trigeminal region. This includes both monosegmental courses affecting the trigeminal region and multisegmental courses involving the trigeminal region, as well as disseminated forms of zoster.
Exclusion criteria:
Patients who were not hospitalized (since the study only includes stationary/inhospital patients).
Patients with Herpes Zoster not involving the trigeminal region (e.g., thoracic, lumbar, or other dermatomes).
Patients treated outside the specified periods (2012–2014 and 2022–2024).
